title: Chapter XIV

teacherSummary.text: Collins praises Lady Catherine at length and explains that he prepares delicate compliments in advance. Asked to read aloud, he picks Fordyce's Sermons and is offended when Lydia interrupts.

significance: Austen mocks rehearsed flattery and moralizing aimed at young women.
discussionQuestions: Why is it funny that Collins prepares compliments in advance?
Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XIV,” how does Austen show pompous flattery? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XIV, how does Austen develop the idea of pompous flattery? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XIV develops the idea of pompous flattery. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XIV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of pompous flattery. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XIV suggests about pompous flattery. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter XIV to complicate the reader's understanding of pompous flattery. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of pompous flattery responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XIV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of pompous flattery follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XIV and its treatment of pompous flattery. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XIV as evidence for a larger claim about pompous flattery in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of pompous flattery. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why is it funny that Collins prepares compliments in advance? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are superintended, backgammon, phaeton, quadrille, resides. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “She is unfortunately of a sickly constitution, which has prevented her making that progress in many accomplishments, which she could not otherwise have failed of; as I am informed by the lady who superintended her education, and who still resides with them.” Webster's says: To have or exercise the charge and oversight of. Now the word history: “superintend”: super- (Latin super, "above") + ten (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “backgammon”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “phaeton”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Fordyce's Sermons to Young Women (1766) was a conduct book on female propriety. Why does this chapter matter? Austen mocks rehearsed flattery and moralizing aimed at young women. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to pompous flattery.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XIV,” how does Austen show pompous flattery? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about pompous flattery, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
